content:
The Pennsylvania Department of Health said it is requesting emergency assistance from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to respond to one of the largest and deadliest measles outbreaks in the country, according to a document reviewed by Reuters on Thursday.

The request comes with a condition requiring the federal agency to recognize four measles-related deaths reported by the state, further inflaming a dispute with the Trump administration.

The state's measles outbreak is at the heart of a standoff between U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro. Kennedy has questioned whether deaths reported in U.S. measles cases since he took office were caused by the virus or other factors, and directed the CDC not to include Pennsylvania's deaths in national statistics.

Public health experts said it is highly unusual for a health secretary to intervene in state health officials' determinations, and it could lead the public to underestimate the risks of measles. Kennedy has accused Shapiro of politicizing the outbreak in his state and of failing to ask for federal help.

In a letter reviewed by Reuters sent by Pennsylvania Health Secretary Debra Bogen to CDC Director Erica Schwartz late Wednesday, the state said it has initiated the process of requesting emergency aid known as an Epi-Aid from the CDC.

Bogen wrote: "The CDC's choice not to publicly confirm these deaths has undermined our response. Therefore, if the CDC cannot transparently and accurately report information about measles-related deaths, the department will withdraw its request for CDC Epi-Aid."

The state health department had previously resisted CDC assistance, saying the outbreak was under control, before making this request.

Grace Davis Jamison, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), said in a statement that the CDC had not received Pennsylvania's request through "normal channels" and that federal outbreak assistance is separate from how the CDC compiles death data.

Jamison said: "The CDC will not give in to this political extortion that uses critical public health assistance as a bargaining chip. The CDC will not allow Governor Shapiro to politicize this process."

Outbreak expands

The state health department said Pennsylvania's outbreak has since expanded rapidly, with confirmed cases rising to more than 700 across 37 counties and four measles-related deaths. The state is the latest to be hit by the worst measles outbreak in the United States in more than three decades, driven by rising vaccine hesitancy and coinciding with President Trump's return to the White House in early 2025.

Shapiro has criticized Kennedy, a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has advocated reducing childhood immunization policies in the United States, for amplifying public concerns about vaccines without scientific basis. Kennedy and Schwartz have in turn blamed Shapiro for not accepting their offer of an Epi-Aid. An Epi-Aid is short-term assistance provided by the CDC during public health emergencies, typically deploying experts to the outbreak for one to three weeks to provide additional support to state and local health departments.

When the Pennsylvania health department announced the first two measles-related deaths on Aug. 25, the disease had sickened 393 people across 28 counties. Shapiro at the time praised his health department's efforts to promote vaccination, while the state health department declined to ask the CDC to send staff to help.

Like other state health departments, Pennsylvania's health department already has long-term CDC staff embedded to help manage outbreaks. A CDC Epi-Aid would be additional federal assistance.

The outbreak has continued to spread, with the pace of new infections accelerating. One death reported this week occurred in Mifflin County, which now has the second-highest number of confirmed cases in the state, more than 100 miles from Lancaster County, where the outbreak originally began.

At the same time, the pace of measles vaccinations provided by the state appears to be slowing, according to health department data. In August, the department administered more than 3,500 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, which provides 97% protection against infection after two doses. By the first half of September, that number had fallen to about 1,100 doses.
